sections.h2: Which New Jersey laws decide a landlord and tenant dispute?
sections.html:
Two statutes cover eviction in New Jersey, and the one that applies depends on the building. According to the New Jersey Courts landlord-tenant page, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 reaches commercial tenants and residential buildings with no more than two rental units, plus a three-family house when the owner lives in one unit. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and the sections after it cover nearly every other residential rental, with hotels, motels and seasonal renters left out.

Cases are filed in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court in the county where the rental sits. A landlord that is a corporation, an LLC or a limited partnership must use a New Jersey attorney, while a sole owner or general partnership may appear without one. Anyone planning to sell a rented house in New Jersey should find out first which statute covers the property, because that choice drives every notice period below.

sections.h2: Can a New Jersey landlord end a tenancy because the house is being sold?
sections.html:
A sale alone is not a reason to remove a tenant in New Jersey. The Anti-Eviction Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1, says a covered tenant can be removed only for a listed cause, and a purchase by an investor leaves the lease in place with the new owner stepping into the landlord's role.

The statute does name a few sale-related grounds. An owner of a building with three residential units or fewer may recover a unit when the owner has contracted to sell to a buyer who wants to live there personally and the contract calls for the unit to be vacant at closing. A condominium or cooperative owner can use a similar ground against tenants whose tenancy began after the master deed was recorded, but only if the tenant received the statement required by N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.9. Other listed grounds include:

  • unpaid rent, or habitual late payment after written notice to stop
  • disorderly conduct or willful damage to the premises
  • a continued breach of reasonable lease covenants or house rules after written notice
  • a refusal of reasonable lease changes at the end of a term
  • a plan to permanently retire the building from residential use
  • conversion of the building to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership

For a seller, the practical point is that a house with a tenant usually sells with the tenant, unless the owner can fit a buyer's own-use contract into the three-unit rule.

sections.h2: How much notice does New Jersey require before a landlord sues?
sections.html:
Notice length depends on the ground, and it runs from three days up to three years. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 requires a written demand and written notice that spells out the cause, delivered in person, left with a family member over 14 at the tenant's home, or sent by certified mail. If the certified letter goes unclaimed, a copy must also go by regular mail. The notice rules do not apply to simple nonpayment of rent.

Notice before suit under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2
GroundNotice before the case is filed
Disorderly conduct, damage to the unit, or certain drug-offence grounds3 days
Rule violations, lease breaches, habitual late rent, or refused lease changes1 month
Owner must board up, demolish or fix cited violations3 months
Owner or buyer will occupy under the sale and own-use grounds2 months, and no suit until a written lease ends
Permanent retirement of the building18 months, and no suit until the lease expires
Conversion to condominium or cooperative3 years, and no suit until the lease expires

Source: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2, published by the New Jersey Department of Community Affairs.

sections.h2: What happens to a tenant's security deposit when the rental is sold?
sections.html:
The seller must hand the deposit and the interest on it to the buyer. Under N.J.S.A. 46:8-20, the owner who conveys the property turns over the deposit plus the tenant's share of interest at the delivery of the deed or within five days after, and notifies the tenant by registered or certified mail with the new owner's name and address. The buyer is then required to collect any deposits and accrued interest from the seller.

Handing the money over releases the seller from liability to the tenant, according to N.J.S.A. 46:8-21. The buyer remains responsible for investing the deposit correctly, giving the required notices, paying interest and returning the money at the end of the lease, even when the seller never transferred it. The state's Security Deposit Law adds several limits that a seller's records should reflect:

  • a deposit may not exceed one and one half months of rent, and later increases may not top 10 percent of the current deposit in a year
  • the landlord must tell the tenant in writing where the money is held, the account type, the interest rate and the amount, and repeat that notice within 30 days of any transfer of ownership
  • nothing may be deducted while the tenant remains in the home
  • the balance, less itemized lawful charges, is due within 30 days after the lease ends
  • a tenant who wins a wrongful-withholding case receives double the amount plus costs, and the Special Civil Part small claims section hears disputes up to $5,000

The law does not cover an owner-occupied building with no more than two rental units unless the tenant gave 30 days' written notice invoking it.

sections.h2: How does a New Jersey eviction case move through court?
sections.html:
An eviction in New Jersey takes a court order and a court officer, and a landlord who skips either step commits an illegal lockout. The landlord files a verified complaint with a landlord case information statement, a copy of the lease and a registration statement. The court lists filing fees of $50 for one defendant and $5 for each extra one, plus a $7 service fee. The trial date is at least 21 days after the summons is served.

A tenant must appear in person, because a written response is not accepted. If the landlord does not appear the case is dismissed, and if the tenant does not appear the case is marked default. When both attend, trained court staff first try a settlement. If there is a trial and the judge rules for the landlord, the result is a judgment for possession. After that, the sequence is:

  • three business days must pass before the landlord may request a warrant of removal, which carries a $35 fee plus mileage
  • a Special Civil Part officer serves the warrant and gives a residential tenant at least three business days to leave
  • the landlord must apply for the warrant within 30 days of the judgment unless a stay or written agreement says otherwise

In a nonpayment case, the tenant can end the matter by paying all rent owed plus lawful costs, even up to three business days after being removed. A landlord who refuses faces a $500 penalty. A tenant may also ask for an orderly removal order of up to seven days, or a hardship stay of up to six months once everything owed is paid.

sections.h2: Which tenant protections complicate a rental sale?
sections.html:
Several defenses can stall a case, and a buyer will usually ask about them before closing. The Courts page lists the habitability doctrine, known in New Jersey as the Marini Doctrine, which lets a tenant who deposits the rent with the court argue that heat, hot water, a working toilet or safe common areas were missing. It cannot be used to excuse a pattern of late rent or lease violations.

Registration matters too. An owner-occupied property with three units or fewer registers with the Community Development Authority, and any other rental registers with the Bureau of Housing Inspection. The registration statement must be filed with the complaint. Tenants may also argue an illegal tenancy, such as an unapproved extra unit, or seek an abatement of rent. A landlord whose tenant receives a rent subsidy must first notify the agency and attach proof to the complaint.

Foreclosure does not erase a lease. A tenant in good standing with a valid lease is not forced out because the building is in foreclosure, and the sheriff's sale purchaser takes the building subject to the tenant's rights.

sections.h2: What should a New Jersey owner gather before selling a rented house?
sections.html:
A seller with tenants should assemble the paperwork a buyer or title agent will ask for. Ask the Special Civil Part office in the county where the property sits for its current fee schedule and forms, since court fees can change. Ask the municipal clerk whether a local rental registration or certificate applies.

  • each signed lease and any renewal, with the rent roll
  • the written deposit notices and the bank record showing where each deposit is held
  • the rental registration statement
  • copies of any notice to cease, notice to quit or court papers
  • repair requests and receipts for work done

A seller who wants the home delivered empty has two honest routes: wait for the lease to end and negotiate a move-out, or sell to a buyer who accepts the tenancy as is.

faqs.q: Can a landlord in New Jersey change the locks to force a tenant out?
faqs.a: No. Only a Special Civil Part officer may carry out an eviction, and only after a judgment for possession and a warrant of removal. Changing locks, padlocking doors or shutting off gas, water or electricity is illegal, and a locked-out tenant can ask the court for readmission and money damages.

faqs.q: Does a tenant have to leave if the landlord sells the house in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Usually not. The lease passes to the buyer. The main exception is a contract with a buyer who will personally occupy a unit in a building of three residential units or fewer and wants it vacant at closing, which requires two months' notice and no suit until a written lease ends.

faqs.q: Who gets the security deposit after a New Jersey rental sells?
faqs.a: The new owner ends up responsible for it. The seller should transfer the deposit with interest at the deed delivery or within five days after, and notify the tenant by certified mail. Even if that step is missed, the buyer must still return the deposit when the lease ends.

faqs.q: How long does a New Jersey landlord have to return a deposit?
faqs.a: Thirty days after the lease ends. The landlord returns the deposit with the tenant's share of interest, less itemized lawful charges, by personal delivery or registered or certified mail. A court that finds the money was wrongly kept awards double the amount plus costs.

faqs.q: Can a tenant stop an eviction after losing in court?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A nonpayment tenant can pay everything owed within three business days of the judgment or even of the eviction. A tenant can also request an order for orderly removal of up to seven days or a hardship stay of up to six months, and requests must reach the court within 10 days of the eviction.
